neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and fully oriented. Anxious but cooperative. Speech fluent and normal.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Normal. Extraocular movements full, pupils equal and reactive. No facial weakness, no ptosis. Bulbar function intact — normal speech and swallowing.
neurological_exam.motor: Symmetric flaccid weakness, legs more than arms. Hip flexion 3/5 bilaterally, knee flexion/extension 4-/5, ankle dorsiflexion 3/5. Shoulder abduction 4/5, grip strength 4-/5 bilaterally. Tone reduced throughout. No fasciculations. Unable to rise from a chair without using the arms.
neurological_exam.sensory: Mild distal paresthesias in the feet and fingertips. Light touch and pinprick mildly reduced in a stocking distribution; vibration mildly reduced at the toes. No sensory level.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Global areflexia — biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, knee, and ankle jerks all absent bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose intact in the arms; leg testing limited by weakness, with no cerebellar signs.
neurological_exam.gait: Unable to walk unassisted — requires support, with a steppage pattern from bilateral foot drop. Romberg deferred due to weakness.
neurological_exam.additional: Bedside spirometry: forced vital capacity (FVC) 2.6 L (~70% predicted), single-breath count 28 — adequate but warrants serial monitoring. Community-acquired pneumonia 3 weeks ago, fully resolved. Received a seasonal influenza vaccine 4 days ago. No fever at presentation. No trauma, no toxic ingestion, no tick exposure, and no recent travel.

patient.chief_complaint: One-week history of progressive, symmetric ascending limb weakness with global areflexia, preceded by pneumonia three weeks earlier.
patient.history_present_illness: A 19-year-old woman presents with one week of progressive limb weakness. Symptoms began with tingling in both feet and difficulty climbing stairs, and over seven days ascended to involve the thighs and then the hands, with mild distal numbness. She now cannot walk without assistance and struggles to rise from a chair. Three weeks ago she had community-acquired pneumonia, treated with a course of oral antibiotics and now fully resolved. Four days ago she received a seasonal influenza vaccine at a campus clinic. She reports no fever, no bladder or bowel dysfunction, no back pain, no diplopia, and no difficulty breathing or swallowing. There is no history of trauma, toxic ingestion, tick exposure, or recent travel. Her maternal grandmother has multiple sclerosis, but there is no family history of hereditary neuropathy. On examination she has symmetric flaccid weakness that is greater in the legs than the arms, mild distal sensory loss in a stocking-glove pattern, and global areflexia — absent reflexes in all four limbs are the critical finding pointing to an acute polyradiculoneuropathy rather than a myelopathy or a functional cause. The combination of subacute, progressive, fairly symmetric ascending weakness with areflexia following an antecedent respiratory infection is the classic presentation of Guillain-Barré syndrome (AIDP). The workup focuses on excluding cord compression and other mimics, confirming the diagnosis with nerve conduction studies and CSF analysis, and monitoring respiratory and autonomic function.

specialized_test.impression: Acute demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy. Prolonged distal motor latencies bilaterally, reduced conduction velocities, partial motor conduction block at the fibular head, temporal dispersion. Absent or prolonged F-waves; H-reflex absent bilaterally. Sural-sparing sensory pattern. Findings are consistent with an acute demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy. Clinical correlation recommended.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Guillain-Barré syndrome, acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (AIDP), post-respiratory infection, seronegative

differential.key_features: No tick exposure and no attached tick on full skin and scalp examination; tick paralysis resolves rapidly after tick removal

differential.diagnosis: Acute transverse myelitis or compressive myelopathy
differential.key_features: Spine MRI shows no cord lesion or compression; areflexia without a sensory level or upper motor neuron signs argues against a cord process
Monophasic course reaching nadir within 4 weeks and a clear antecedent infection favour GBS; CIDP would progress beyond 8 weeks or relapse
Descending rather than ascending pattern, prominent bulbar and autonomic onset, and pupillary involvement; no toxin or food source identified
Blood lead level normal and urine toxicology negative; no toxic exposure history

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Monitored admission for respiratory and autonomic surveillance

critical_actions: Monitor respiratory function with serial bedside FVC — intubate before overt respiratory failure (FVC below ~15-20 mL/kg, a rapid downward trend, or bulbar compromise); SpO2 can remain normal until decompensation
Treat with IVIG 2 g/kg total over 5 days OR plasma exchange — both are equally effective first-line therapies
Monitor for autonomic instability — labile blood pressure, arrhythmia, ileus — with continuous telemetry during the progressive phase

Confirm the diagnosis and exclude compressive myelopathy before attributing the weakness to GBS — global areflexia plus a demyelinating NCS pattern and CSF albuminocytologic dissociation establish the diagnosis
contraindicated_actions: Corticosteroids — ineffective in GBS and not recommended
Succinylcholine if intubation is required — risk of hyperkalemia; use a non-depolarising agent such as rocuronium
Discharging the patient home — GBS can progress rapidly to respiratory failure and requires monitored admission
key_reasoning_points: Progressive, fairly symmetric ascending weakness with global areflexia following an antecedent infection is the classic presentation of GBS (AIDP)
CSF albuminocytologic dissociation — elevated protein with a normal cell count — is characteristic; it may be absent in the first few days but is typically present by the end of the first week
Respiratory failure is the main acute danger; serial FVC monitoring, not SpO2, detects impending decompensation
An antecedent respiratory infection (here, pneumonia 3 weeks prior) is the most likely trigger; vaccines are a rare trigger and, when implicated, GBS is managed identically
A negative anti-ganglioside panel does not exclude GBS — a substantial proportion of AIDP cases are seronegative
A maternal-line history of multiple sclerosis does not indicate hereditary neuropathy and confers no increased genetic risk for GBS

red_herrings.data_point: Seasonal influenza vaccine received 4 days before symptom onset
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute the GBS to the recent vaccine and delay the search for the true antecedent trigger
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Vaccines are a rare GBS trigger; the community-acquired pneumonia 3 weeks earlier is the far more likely antecedent. Either way, GBS is treated identically with IVIG or plasma exchange — establishing causation does not change acute management.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest a hereditary or central demyelinating process and broaden the workup toward multiple sclerosis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: GBS is a peripheral, post-infectious immune-mediated disorder, not a heritable or central demyelinating disease; a family history of MS is not relevant to this presentation.

metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward adult AIDP — classic progressive ascending weakness with areflexia after an antecedent respiratory infection; confirmed by demyelinating NCS and CSF albuminocytologic dissociation; a recent influenza vaccine is a red herring
